reason: Year and country hold: China's first full-functional international Internet connection is a real, well-documented event dated 20 April 1994, at 64 Kbps, marking it the "77th country" with full internet access (per China's own official histories: CNNIC, China Internet Museum, and the Chinese Academy of Sciences). However, the description's specific actor detail — "a 64 Kbps line to Stanford University" — conflates two distinct 1994-era connections. The officially recognized 20 April 1994 full-internet milestone was a 64K international dedicated line from NCFC (National Computing and Networking Facility of China) routed via Sprint Corporation (a US carrier), NOT a direct line to Stanford. Separately, a 64 Kbps line between the Institute of High Energy Physics (IHEP) and Stanford's SLAC (Stanford Linear Accelerator Center) existed from March 1993 as a narrower physics-research link, explicitly described by Chinese sources as only a "partial" internet connection at that stage, though SLAC's own history and some Western press (e.g., CNN, Symmetry Magazine) frame the IHEP-SLAC link's full TCP/IP activation (~March-May 1994) as "the first Internet connection to mainland China" — a competing but less officially-cited narrative. Given the genuine, sourced ambiguity in which specific line is "the" first full connection, but clear confirmation that Stanford/SLAC's role was a separate, narrower physics-institution link rather than the nationwide gateway most sources credit, this is a material actor/scope discrepancy rather than a clean match. Core facts (China, 1994, ~64 Kbps, first full internet access) are solidly confirmed; the "Stanford University" attribution is a commonly repeated but contested simplification.

Core fact (country/year/action) is solid, so this clears the TRUE bar rather than PARTIAL.

title: Gallium and germanium export controls — tech war escalation
reason: China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and General Administration of Customs jointly announced on July 3, 2023 export control measures on gallium- and germanium-related items (gallium metal, gallium nitride, gallium arsenide, germanium metal, germanium dioxide, etc.), with the controls taking effect August 1, 2023. Exporters had to obtain licenses for these materials, which are critical inputs for semiconductors, solar panels, and defense/electronics applications. Multiple independent legal/trade-policy analyses (Mayer Brown, Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, Winston & Strawn, CSIS) and the IEA describe this as a direct response to escalating US semiconductor export restrictions on China, marking the first time Chinese critical-minerals controls were explicitly tied to retaliation in the US-China tech war. Real-world trade data confirms material effect: gallium/germanium wrought exports dropped to zero in August 2023 versus thousands of kg in July, and gallium prices rose ~27% following the announcement. All elements of the description (country=China, year=2023, materials, retaliatory motive, tech-war escalation framing) are corroborated.
